questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing a finding with a differently sampled rate
questions.learningObjective: Bound a comparison between a finding and a rate
questions.stem: In a cartographer's projection, a survey result is set beside a regional rate, and the workshop asks how far the comparison holds.

options.text: Only as two separate readings, since the survey's group and the rate's group were drawn differently.
As a direct comparison, because a survey result and a regional rate describe the same area of interest.
options.misconception: ignores how the two samples were formed

options.text: As a direct comparison, because the survey was careful and the rate is the less reliable of the two.
options.misconception: ranks sources by neatness rather than by sample

options.text: Not at all, because a regional rate and a survey result can never be placed on the same sheet.
options.misconception: believes two unlike figures cannot share a figure

questions.explanation: Two figures drawn together can still fail to compare, when they came from differently drawn groups. The sheet can show them side by side, but comparison needs matching samples.
questions.hint: Ask how each group was chosen.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A case set against a rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain the licence a case set against a rate carries
questions.stem: A mapping project sets a single surveyed valley against a national average, and the note asks for the explanation of the licence.

answer.exemplar: The valley was surveyed in detail and can be described in detail, while the national average describes a country-wide population of which the valley is one case. Placing them side by side on a sheet invites the reader to treat the valley as a version of the average, which reverses the relationship. The note therefore states what each figure describes and labels the valley as a case rather than as a scaled-down average.

questions.explanation: A detailed case and a broad average are different kinds of figure. Setting them side by side invites the reader to treat the case as a small average, so the note labels each one.
questions.hint: Ask what each figure describes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming the two fields a question joins
questions.learningObjective: Name the fields a map overlay actually joins

stimulus.body: A projection note describes a thematic map that shades each district by the elevation of its highest point and overlays the locations of schools. The mapmaker asks what the two layers actually bring together and which key makes the overlay possible.

questions.stem: A map overlays two layers, and the workshop asks what the pairing actually joins.

options.text: Elevation and school location, since an overlay on a sheet is by definition a comparison of them.
options.misconception: assumes an overlay always compares the two quantities shown

options.text: A district-level attribute with a point location, joined by the district each point falls inside.
The two layers are independent, since an overlay is a display choice and joins no data at all.
options.misconception: believes a map display involves no data join

options.text: The school locations with the terrain they stand on, since that is what a reader of the sheet will want.
options.misconception: assumes the reader's interest defines the join

questions.explanation: An overlay becomes meaningful once two layers are brought onto a common key, and here a point meets a district. Naming that key turns a picture of two layers into a question the map can answer.
questions.hint: Ask what identifies the link between the layers.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared artefact used for different purposes
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what sharing an artefact gains and costs
questions.stem: Two institutes use the same boundary file for their own purposes, and the workshop asks what sharing it allows and costs.

options.text: It lets both speak about the same places, and costs nothing, since the file is only a list of coordinates.
options.misconception: assumes a shared artefact carries no interpretation

options.text: It allows each institute to keep its own definitions, and costs nothing, since the list can be read any way.
options.misconception: believes a shared file leaves each user's meaning intact

options.text: It lets both talk about the same places, and it costs each the right to define those places its own way.
It allows both to publish at once, and it costs each institute the ability to correct errors independently.
options.misconception: treats a shared file as a permanent loss of independence

questions.explanation: A shared boundary file gives two institutes a common referent, so their maps can be read against each other. The price is that the definition of a place becomes a matter of agreement, not one choice.
questions.hint: Ask what both institutes now take for granted.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a boundary object allows each field to do
questions.learningObjective: State what a boundary object permits and what must be recorded
questions.stem: First decide what the shared object lets each side do with it, then state what the workshop must record.

options.text: It lets each side read the other's data, so the record must list the fields that are exchanged.
options.misconception: reduces a boundary object to a data channel

options.text: It lets each side draw its own conclusions, so the record must state that neither side is accountable.
options.misconception: treats shared use as shared exemption

options.text: It lets each side produce a joint map, so the record must name the scale of the joint output.
options.misconception: assumes the only shared purpose is a joint product

options.text: It lets each side use the other's meaning without renegotiating it, so the record must fix that meaning.

questions.explanation: A boundary object lets each field act without renegotiating the other, which works only if the shared meaning is fixed. The record is where that meaning is written down.
questions.hint: Ask what each side may assume without asking.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared vocabulary and who it serves
questions.learningObjective: Identify who a shared vocabulary serves
questions.stem: A mapping agency adopts one term for a feature that two surveys had named differently, and the workshop asks who the term now serves.

options.text: The office publishing the atlas, since a shared term makes the printed sheets consistent.
Every field that reads the sheets, since a term that means one thing can only be understood one way by all.
options.misconception: assumes a shared term produces a shared understanding

options.text: Whichever survey used the term first, since the earlier usage carries the priority in a naming dispute.
options.misconception: believes priority in time settles a naming question

options.text: Nobody in particular, since a term is only a label and carries no obligations on those who adopt it.
options.misconception: believes a label imposes no duty on its users

questions.explanation: A shared term standardises the sheets it appears on, and the agency publishing them gains most. Other fields gain a usable cross-reference but inherit a definition they did not write and may not need.
questions.hint: Ask whose problem the shared term solves first.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A common unit of description
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two different units cannot share one scale
questions.stem: A projection mixes a distance measure from one survey with an area measure from another, and the note asks for the explanation of the mismatch.

answer.exemplar: A distance in kilometres and an area in square kilometres share a word but not a quantity, and a legend that places them side by side invites the reader to treat them as comparable. The projection cannot convert one into the other without knowing a density, which is a third piece of information about the same ground. The note therefore keeps the two measurements in separate panels and says plainly that no comparison between them was made.

questions.explanation: A linear measure and an area measure share a name but not a quantity, and no conversion exists without a density. The projection keeps them in separate panels and says no comparison was made.
questions.hint: Ask what would be needed to convert one into the other.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing a finding with a differently sampled rate
questions.learningObjective: Compare a point measurement with a modelled rate

stimulus.body: A projection note places a gauge reading taken at one site beside a modelled rate computed over a whole river basin. The gauge is in the middle of the basin and the model was fitted on a decade of records from the basin's larger tributaries. The mapmaker asks what the two marks can be compared for.

questions.stem: A point measurement is drawn beside a modelled rate, and the workshop asks what the two marks support.

options.text: A direct comparison, because the gauge site lies inside the basin and so represents the modelled rate.
options.misconception: assumes location inside an area makes a point representative

options.text: Nothing beyond showing where a reading and a model coincide, since one is a sample of one place.
A calibration of the model, because a single site is enough to check a model fitted to a whole basin.
options.misconception: believes one point can validate a basin-wide model

options.text: A trend, because the gauge series and the model output together give the basin's change over time.
options.misconception: reads a paired snapshot as a change over time

questions.explanation: A gauge at one site and a model for a basin answer different questions, and the model's fit shows how far one site can be trusted. The sheet can show agreement without treating the reading as a test.
questions.hint: Ask what each mark was made to describe.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A case set against a rate
questions.learningObjective: Combine an exception sheet with a rate sheet
questions.stem: One sheet treats a boundary case as an exception, and another measures it against a rate, and the editor asks how to combine them.

options.text: Keep the exception sheet, because an exception is more informative than any rate the other sheet can offer.
options.misconception: prefers a narrative case over a measured figure

options.text: Keep the rate sheet, because a rate is a stronger kind of statement than a description of one case.
options.misconception: ranks a rate above a case simply by its form

options.text: Show the case and the rate separately, so the reader sees both without a false pairing.
Blend them, since a note that keeps them apart gives the reader two answers to one question.
options.misconception: avoids clarity to appear to answer a single question

questions.explanation: An exception and a rate answer different questions, and a figure that combines them invites the reader to treat the case as an instance of the rate. Keeping them visibly separate preserves both.
questions.hint: Ask what each element was put on the sheet to do.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming the two fields a question joins
questions.learningObjective: Name the joined fields and their key
questions.stem: First name the two fields the question joins, then say which key makes the join possible.

options.text: A road layer and a census layer, joined by the census district that each road segment falls in.
options.misconception: names a pairing the question does not require

options.text: A rainfall layer and a soil layer, joined by the field identifier carried on both sources.
options.misconception: joins fields that share a technical key but not a question

options.text: An elevation layer and a rainfall layer, joined by the point where the two rasters intersect.
options.misconception: treats a raster overlap as a single identifying key

options.text: A settlement layer and a flood extent layer, joined by the settlement point inside the flooded area.

questions.explanation: A join is right only when its two fields are the ones the question is about, and the key must identify one place in both. A key that links convenient layers produces a number for a different question.
questions.hint: Ask what place both layers must describe.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared artefact used for different purposes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what reusing a raster commits a team to
questions.stem: A land-use raster is reused by an insurance team for a different purpose, and the workshop asks what the reuse commits them to.

options.text: That the classes mean what the original survey recorded, since a raster carries its own class definitions.
Nothing, because a raster is only a grid of values and carries no definition of what the values are.
options.misconception: believes a data file can be free of meaning

options.text: That their own classes are compatible, since two land-use schemes with the same cell size can be compared.
options.misconception: assumes a shared grid makes schemes comparable

options.text: That the survey date is irrelevant, because the classes describe the land rather than the year it was seen.
options.misconception: believes a land class is independent of when it was observed

questions.explanation: A raster carries the classification scheme it was made under, and reusing it means working inside that scheme. The insurance team inherits the survey's class definitions and date, fit or not.
questions.hint: Ask what the class labels were defined against.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a boundary object allows each field to do
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a boundary object permits each party to do
questions.stem: A boundary object is shared by a survey office and a local authority, and the note asks for the explanation of what each may do with it.

answer.exemplar: The shared object is a settlement boundary file that both parties have agreed means the same thing. Because the definition is settled, the survey office can count population inside it and the local authority can apply its own rules to the same places, and neither has to re-derive what the boundary is. What neither may do is treat the file as evidence about the other party's area, since the agreement covered the meaning of the boundary and not the truth of what lies inside it.

questions.explanation: A boundary object works because its meaning is agreed, letting each side act on the same referent. The agreement covers the definition, not the conclusions each side draws.
questions.hint: Ask what the agreement actually covered.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared vocabulary and who it serves
questions.learningObjective: Identify the audience a place-name standard serves

stimulus.body: A place-name committee has agreed a single term for a feature that two map series had named differently, and the sheets from both series will carry it from the next edition. The committee's paper says only that the sheets should agree. The cartographer asks whom the standard actually serves.

questions.stem: A place-name committee standardises a term used by two map series, and the cartographer asks whom the standard serves.

options.text: The committee, since the body that defines the term is the one that gains most from a common usage.
options.misconception: assumes the definer gains most from standardisation

options.text: Readers who use both series, since a shared term lets them match a name in one sheet against the other.
The larger series, since a standard term adopted by a big series will be adopted by the small one anyway.
options.misconception: lets scale decide a naming standard

options.text: The cartographers, since consistent naming makes the work of drawing and checking easier for them.
options.misconception: confuses the producer's convenience with the reader's need

questions.explanation: A place-name standard earns its keep with readers who hold more than one series, since a name in one sheet can be found in the other. The cartographers gain tidiness, but tidiness was never scarce.
questions.hint: Ask who holds more than one version of the information.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A common unit of description
questions.learningObjective: Decide which conversion a map may honestly make
questions.stem: Two datasets describe the same phenomenon in different units, and the workshop asks what conversion the map can honestly make.

options.text: Convert one into the other, since a conversion is arithmetic and arithmetic carries no interpretation.
options.misconception: believes unit conversion is free of interpretation

options.text: Convert both into a third unit, since a common unit removes the need to choose between them.
options.misconception: assumes a third unit sidesteps the choice of definition

options.text: Convert only where the underlying quantity is the same, and otherwise keep both figures separate.
Convert nothing, since any two units of a quantity can always be compared once converted.
options.misconception: believes all units of a thing are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Conversion is legitimate only when the two numbers measure the same quantity, and a shared name does not guarantee that. Where the quantities differ, a converted figure answers a different question.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two figures count the same thing.

questions.topic: Comparing a finding with a differently sampled rate
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a side-by-side pairing of two results licenses
questions.stem: A projection compares a study's finding with a rate taken from a different sample, and the cartographer asks what the map shows.

options.text: It shows the study's finding, because a study is a stronger source of evidence than a regional rate.
options.misconception: ranks a source by kind instead of by what it measured

options.text: It shows the regional rate, because a rate covers more ground than any single study can.
options.misconception: confuses breadth of coverage with strength of evidence

options.text: It shows both, because placing the two together lets a reader weigh them against each other.
options.misconception: assumes juxtaposition is a way of settling a comparison

options.text: It shows two separate results, since a finding and a differently sampled rate are not a comparison.

questions.explanation: Two things drawn together are not a comparison, because a finding and a differently sampled rate answer different questions. The map can carry both, but the legend must say they are not one measure.
questions.hint: Ask what question each figure was collected to answer.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A case set against a rate
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a case sits inside a rated population
questions.stem: A thematic map sets a single province's yield against a country rate, and the note asks for the explanation of the comparison.

answer.exemplar: The province's yield was measured over its own fields in one season, and the country rate was computed from a survey of farms drawn to represent the whole country. The two figures are about different populations of fields, and the province is a member of the country population rather than a rival to it. A chart that sets them side by side as though the province were competing with the average misstates the relationship, so the note treats the province as one member of the population the rate describes.

questions.explanation: A measured case and a population rate are not rivals, because the case belongs to the population the rate describes. The note states the relationship so a difference is not read as a contest.
questions.hint: Ask how the case sits inside the population.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming the two fields a question joins
questions.learningObjective: Name the fields a modelled surface joins to points

stimulus.body: A projection note describes a map that colours each district by the soil moisture a model computes for it, and prints a marker for every borehole in the district. The mapmaker asks which two fields the map actually joins, since the model works over cells and the boreholes are points.

questions.stem: A modelled surface and a set of points are drawn together, and the workshop asks which fields the map joins.

options.text: Soil moisture and borehole depth, because a marker on a moisture map reads as a measurement of the soil.
options.misconception: reads the overlay as if the two measurements were the same

options.text: Modelled moisture by district and borehole locations, joined through the cell each point falls in.
Nothing, since a model over cells and a set of point locations cannot be shown on one sheet.
options.misconception: believes two spatial forms cannot share a figure

options.text: Borehole readings and model output, because a point inside a cell is a check on the model there.
options.misconception: assumes the overlay reports a validation result

questions.explanation: A modelled surface and a set of points are joined by placing each point in a cell, and the map shows a model field with observations. Calling it a check would claim a comparison the map never made.
questions.hint: Ask what links a point to a modelled cell.

questions.topic: A shared artefact used for different purposes
questions.learningObjective: Separate the needs of two users of one basemap
questions.stem: One team uses a shared basemap for navigation and another for statistics, and the workshop asks what each needs from it.

options.text: Navigation needs position and legibility, statistics need stable areas, and the basemap must serve both.
Both need a picture of the ground, and a single basemap can be drawn once and used for every purpose.
options.misconception: assumes one rendering can serve every use

options.text: The first needs accuracy and the second needs speed, so the workshop should build two separate basemaps.
options.misconception: assumes a conflict of needs forces separate products

options.text: Neither needs anything special, since a basemap is a background and the real content sits on top of it.
options.misconception: treats a basemap as decoration with no requirements

questions.explanation: A shared basemap is asked to serve two kinds of work, and navigation and statistics want different things. Naming what each side needs lets the workshop decide whether one artefact holds both.
questions.hint: Ask what each use would fail without.

questions.topic: What a boundary object allows each field to do
questions.learningObjective: State the permission and the prohibition in a shared layer
questions.stem: First state what the shared layer permits on one side, then state what it forbids on the other.

options.text: It permits the agency to publish the other agency's data, and it forbids that agency from correcting errors.
options.misconception: treats a shared licence as a transfer of control

options.text: It permits each side to use the other's agreed features, and it forbids either side from redefining them.
It permits each side to extend the layer for its own use, and it forbids the other side from seeing them.
options.misconception: treats independent extension as a permitted use

options.text: It permits one side to set the layer's content, and it forbids the other side from asking for changes.
options.misconception: lets one side's need set the shared terms

questions.explanation: A shared layer works when each side can rely on the other's features meaning what the agreement says. Any side that redefines those features breaks the reliance sharing was meant to create.
questions.hint: Ask what each side takes for granted about the other.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared vocabulary and who it serves
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a shared vocabulary costs its readers
questions.stem: A glossary gives one word to two land-cover types, and the editor asks what a shared vocabulary costs the readers.

options.text: Nothing, since a glossary is what removes the need to learn a separate term for each feature.
options.misconception: assumes a glossary removes the ambiguity it handles

options.text: Some precision, since a reader wanting the finer distinction can consult the survey's own scheme.
options.misconception: treats a loss as recoverable by looking elsewhere

options.text: The distinction itself, because a reader who knows one word for two classes cannot tell which is shown.
Nothing much, because both classes are usually present and the reader can see the difference on the ground.
options.misconception: assumes the reader can resolve a class label visually

questions.explanation: One word for two classes removes the ability to say which class is meant, a loss for a reader who must act on the map. The glossary helps producers agree while making the output less precise.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can no longer distinguish.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A common unit of description
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a mixed legend invites a reader to infer
questions.stem: A map legend mixes a linear scale with a categorical band, and the note asks for the explanation of the unit problem.

answer.exemplar: A linear scale says that twice the distance along it means twice the quantity, so a reader can interpolate and reason about differences. A categorical band says only that a value falls in a named class, so nothing follows from one band being next to another. Putting both in one legend invites a reader to treat a band boundary as a threshold they can reason about, which is a stronger claim than the classification supports. The note separates the two and says which readings each one permits.

questions.explanation: A linear scale supports interpolation and a categorical band does not, so a band edge read as a threshold is a mistake. The note keeps the two apart and says what each supports.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can infer between two classes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing a finding with a differently sampled rate
questions.learningObjective: Bound a visual pairing of a case and a national rate

stimulus.body: A projection note sets a detailed survey of one river valley beside a national rate for the same indicator. The valley survey used every holding in the valley, while the national rate was computed from a sample of holdings selected to represent the country. The mapmaker asks what the visual pairing licenses a reader to conclude.

questions.stem: A valley survey is drawn beside a national rate, and the workshop asks what the pairing licenses.

options.text: That the valley differs from the national figure, since a full survey is more accurate than a sampled rate.
options.misconception: compares two figures without checking what each covers

options.text: Little, since one figure covers every holding in a valley and the other a sample chosen for the country.
That the valley is unusual, since a case set beside a national rate is a comparison by design.
options.misconception: assumes juxtaposition signals a contrast to be drawn

options.text: That the valley rate is the national rate for that area, because the valley is part of the country population.
options.misconception: treats a national estimate as applying to a part of it

questions.explanation: One figure covers all holdings in a valley and the other a sample chosen to represent a country, so they estimate different things. Treating the valley as the country's case there borrows a number.
questions.hint: Ask what population each figure was computed for.

questions.topic: A case set against a rate
questions.learningObjective: Separate a district rate from a claim of typicality
questions.stem: A map shades a single district by its own rate while a note calls it typical of the country, and the editor asks what holds.

options.text: The shading describes that district, and the typicality claim needs evidence covering the country.
The shading and the note agree, since a district rate from many records is reliably typical of a country.
options.misconception: assumes a large count makes a district representative

options.text: Neither holds, because a district that can be shaded cannot be described without national comparators.
options.misconception: denies any description of a district in isolation

options.text: The note holds if the district is named, since naming a case makes the reader judge its typicality.
options.misconception: believes naming a case licenses a claim about the whole

questions.explanation: A district rate describes that district, and calling it typical is a claim about a country its figures do not support. Naming the district locates the case but does not settle representativeness.
questions.hint: Ask what population the typicality claim is about.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the pairing a question actually requires
questions.stem: Two maps answer the same question with different pairings of layers, and the workshop asks which pairing the question requires.

options.text: Whichever layers are most complete, since a fuller dataset produces a more reliable answer to any question.
options.misconception: judges a pairing by data volume rather than by meaning

options.text: Whichever pairing the earlier map used, since changing approach mid-programme makes the sheets inconsistent.
options.misconception: keeps a method for the sake of consistency

options.text: The pairing whose two fields are the question's own, since a join answers a question or it does not.
The pairing with the finer resolution, because finer data always supports a more precise statement.
options.misconception: believes finer resolution settles what a question requires

options.misconception: assumes a shared dataset has uniform accuracy

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a boundary object allows each field to do
questions.learningObjective: Explain what each party may assume about a shared file
questions.stem: A shared place-name file is used by a mapmaker and a delivery company, and the note asks for the explanation of what each may assume.

answer.exemplar: The place-name file was assembled so that a road, a settlement and a delivery point can be matched to one another across both organisations. The mapmaker may therefore assume that a name in the file denotes the same feature the delivery company will route to, and the delivery company may assume the mapmaker's rendering of that feature refers to the same place. Neither may assume anything about how current the file is, because freshness was not part of what the two sides agreed to share.

questions.explanation: A shared name file supports matching one feature across two organisations, and each side may rely on that. The agreement was about identity, not attributes like currency that nobody guaranteed.
questions.hint: Ask what the file was assembled to match.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the cost of reusing an artefact for a new question

answer.exemplar: The artefact was produced for a question about boundaries, and the planning office now uses it to decide where a new service should go, which is a different question with different consequences. Because the reuse is undocumented, the researcher assumes the artefact reflects a settled administrative position, and the planning office assumes the researcher knows the limitations. Each side is reading the artefact's silence as agreement, which is exactly the risk that a shared object carries.

options.text: It permits each to use the agreed features, and it does not permit either to treat the file as current.
It permits the national agency to publish and the county to draft, since ownership decides the standing.
options.misconception: assumes ownership settles the right to publish

options.text: It permits nothing until maintenance is agreed, since a file without an owner cannot be used at all.
options.misconception: treats an unsettled duty as blocking all use

questions.explanation: The agreement fixed what the boundaries mean, and that is what each side can rely on. It says nothing about whether the survey is current, so neither side may present the file as current.

answer.exemplar: The measured outcome came from the handful of sites a survey team visited, and the rate came from a register covering a much larger area. A figure for a visited site and a rate for an area are two estimates of two populations, and the difference between them may reflect the difference between the populations rather than any difference in performance. The note therefore presents the measured outcome as a description of the sites visited and keeps the rate labelled as an area estimate, without setting one against the other.

questions.explanation: A measured outcome and an area rate are two estimates of two populations, and the gap between them may reflect the populations rather than performance. The note keeps each labelled for what it is.

options.misconception: treats shared provenance as shared representativeness

Nothing, because a case of any size cannot be set against a national rate on a single sheet.

options.text: That the two districts are exceptional, since a case drawn next to a rate is meant to stand out from it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain whom a harmonising vocabulary serves
questions.stem: A shared vocabulary is introduced to harmonise two atlases, and the note asks for the explanation of whom it serves.

answer.exemplar: The vocabulary exists so that a reader who moves from one atlas to the other can carry a name across and find the same place. It does not exist to make the two atlases look alike, and it is not a classification scheme for either of them, since it leaves the underlying surveys' own categories in place. The atlas that adopts a term second is the one making the larger concession, and the note should record which side changed what and why the reader's convenience was the reason.

questions.explanation: A shared vocabulary is built for readers who cross between products, and it imposes no classification on either survey. The side that changes second concedes more, and the note records that trade.

questions.learningObjective: Name the fields a land-cover question joins
questions.stem: A question about land cover joins a satellite classification to a cadastral layer, and the workshop asks what the join names.

options.text: The classified ground cover and the registered parcels, joined on the parcels inside each classified patch.
The satellite and the cadastral office, joined on the year in which each last updated its records.
options.misconception: joins two sources rather than two fields

options.text: Only the parcels, since land cover is an attribute of a parcel and not a layer in its own right.
options.misconception: reduces a layer to an attribute of another

options.text: The two areas, since joining land cover to parcels simply combines the shapes of both into one outline.
options.misconception: treats a join as a geometric union

questions.explanation: A join names the two fields a result is about: ground cover and registered parcels, matched by which parcels fall in which patch. Naming anything else produces a result for a question nobody asked.
questions.hint: Ask what one record of the result describes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared artefact used for different purposes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what republishing with different metadata creates
questions.stem: A shared dataset is republished by two agencies with different metadata, and the workshop asks what the sharing has created.

options.text: Nothing, because the underlying data are identical and metadata is only description added afterwards.
options.misconception: treats metadata as inert decoration on data

options.text: Two versions of the same data with different meanings, since each agency describes fields in its own terms.
A standard, since republishing the same data is how a shared description becomes official.
options.misconception: treats republication as the creation of agreement

options.text: A dependency, since both agencies now depend on the original publisher and cannot revise the data.
options.misconception: believes reuse removes the right to correct

questions.explanation: Republishing the same data with different metadata produces two things that look alike and mean differently. That is a new artefact nobody designed, so the workshop must record the versions and terms.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two descriptions agree.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a boundary object allows each field to do
questions.learningObjective: Say what each party gains from a shared definition

stimulus.body: A projection note describes a boundary object that carries a shared definition of a district used by a national survey office for reporting and by a health board for allocating funds. The two bodies agreed the districts and their meaning, and the survey office supplies the figures the health board then applies its own formula to. The cartographer asks what each body has gained.

questions.stem: A shared definition is used by a survey office and a health board, and the workshop asks what each has gained.

options.text: The survey office has gained a second audience, and the health board has gained a definition it did not write.
options.misconception: credits the definer with a second audience, not the reader

options.text: Both have gained nothing, since a shared definition is an arrangement and no new facts were produced.
options.misconception: believes sharing produces no informational gain

options.text: The office has gained a common referent for its figures, and the board a settled way to apply its formula.
The health board has gained independence, since it can apply its formula without asking the office.
options.misconception: describes dependence as if it were independence

questions.explanation: A shared definition lets the survey office state its figures about the places the board funds, and lets the board apply its formula without renegotiating. Neither side gained the other's judgement.
questions.hint: Ask what each side can now do without asking the other.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared vocabulary and who it serves
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a split usage of one term produces
questions.stem: A term is adopted for one feature on a sheet but keeps its old sense in a gazetteer, and the editor asks what the split has produced.

options.text: Two meanings under one word, so a reader who moves between the products cannot tell which sense is meant.
A clean separation, since the sheet and the gazetteer are separate documents and readers know which is which.
options.misconception: believes readers always know which document they hold

options.text: A consistent usage, since keeping the old sense in the gazetteer preserves the term's history on the sheet.
options.misconception: treats a split usage as preserving consistency

options.text: No effect, since a place name in a gazetteer and a label on a sheet are different kinds of object entirely.
options.misconception: believes the two uses cannot meet in one reader's mind

questions.explanation: A term that means one thing on the sheet and another in the gazetteer leaves a reader unable to tell which is meant. The split must be closed by disambiguating the sheet or retiring the old sense.
questions.hint: Ask which document a reader has open.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A common unit of description
questions.learningObjective: Explain what two different denominators in one legend imply
questions.stem: A projection reports a rate per square kilometre and a density per household, and the cartographer asks what the legend implies.

options.text: That the two figures are comparable, since both are densities and densities can be set side by side.
options.misconception: treats two denominators as one kind of measure

options.text: That the two layers divide by different things, since one is per square kilometre and one per household.
That the household figure is more precise, since counting households is a more direct measure than area.
options.misconception: ranks two denominators by how direct they feel

options.text: That a household can be treated as a fixed area, so the two rates can be converted into one another.
options.misconception: assumes a fixed size for households

questions.explanation: Two rates dividing by different things describe two quantities, and a legend holding both invites a forbidden comparison. Converting one into the other needs a household size the projection lacks.
questions.hint: Ask what each rate divides by.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing a finding with a differently sampled rate
questions.learningObjective: Write one wording that serves two sheets with different limits
questions.stem: Two sheets compare a finding with a rate in different ways, and the editor asks for one wording that stays inside both limits.

options.text: Compare the finding with the rate directly, since the reader will do it anyway and better to do it first.
options.misconception: concedes a comparison to keep the reader on the page

options.text: Report the finding alone, since a rate drawn from another sample adds nothing that can be used.
options.misconception: discards usable material to avoid the comparison

options.text: Report each figure for the group it covers, and say that the sheet does not compare them.
Report the rate alone, since it covers more people and therefore supersedes a small finding.
options.misconception: lets coverage decide which figure to drop

questions.explanation: Both sheets stay inside their limits while each figure is labelled for the group it covers. The wording must say that no comparison is made, since two adjacent figures will be compared anyway.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader will do with two figures.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A case set against a rate
questions.learningObjective: Assign the case and the rate their separate roles
questions.stem: First decide what the case contributes, then state what the rate can carry beside it.

options.text: The case contributes a rate, and the rate may then be quoted for every area with the same profile.
options.misconception: turns a single case into a transferable figure

options.text: The case contributes nothing measurable, and the rate may stand alone as the sheet's only figure.
options.misconception: denies a case any evidential role at all

options.text: The case contributes the rate, and the two may be used together to give the rate a wider scope.
options.misconception: uses a case to enlarge the scope of a rate

options.text: The case contributes character, and the rate can carry size for the wider population beside it.

questions.explanation: A case shows what something is like and a rate shows how much of it there is, and each stays inside its reach on a shared sheet. A case used to widen a rate turns a description into a number.
questions.hint: Ask what each element can show on its own.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming the two fields a question joins
questions.learningObjective: Identify the key a join between two spatial layers requires
questions.stem: A query needs a road layer and a catchment layer, and the workshop asks which key the join requires.

options.text: A key that identifies the same location in both, since the join has to place a road inside a catchment.
The road's own identifier, since a catchment can always be attached to a road by naming it on the sheet.
options.misconception: believes a label can substitute for a spatial match

options.text: The catchments' codes, since a road crossing several catchments must be recorded under all of them.
options.misconception: turns a location match into a code list

options.text: No key, since a road and a catchment meet in the ground and the software can find the overlap itself.
options.misconception: believes a spatial match needs no agreed key

questions.explanation: A join needs a key naming the same place in both layers, because the result is a statement about a road inside a catchment. A key that only links labels produces a result about something else.
questions.hint: Ask what the joined result is a statement about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A shared artefact used for different purposes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a shared artefact permits its two users to do
questions.stem: A shared artefact serves two studios with different purposes, and the note asks for the explanation of what it permits.

answer.exemplar: The artefact is a set of generalised coastlines that one studio uses for illustration and the other uses for tidal work, and the generalisation suits the first purpose while making the second unsafe. A shared artefact does not need its users to have the same purpose, but it does need each use to stay inside what the artefact's own precision allows. The note therefore records the level at which the artefact was generalised, and the studio that needs more must commission more rather than assume it.

questions.explanation: A shared artefact can serve two purposes provided each use stays inside the precision it actually has. The note records that precision, so a user who needs more must commission more.
questions.hint: Ask what the artefact's own level allows.
